A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same egoPPG research, dataset, and downstream application. Both complete 16-page documents, including supplementary text, equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original heart-rate estimation experiments, EgoExo4D proficiency results, and supplementary hyperparameter analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original heart-rate and proficiency experiments, component ablations, cross-dataset evaluations, and supplementary comparisons of downstream HR sources.

M1.justification: EgoPulseFormer becomes PulseFormer and gains motion-informed temporal attention using the headset IMU. A new ResNet18 image-embedding branch and convolutional IMU embeddings feed cross-attention that weights video frames before the retained spatial-attention CNN backbone (Section 5.2). This changes the inputs and computation substantially.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on MMPD, UBFC-rPPG, and PURE through bidirectional transfer with egoPPG-DB (Supplementary Section 16). These introduce conventional facial-video domains beyond the retained egoPPG-DB and EgoExo4D experiments. OBF and SCAMPS are added only to the related-dataset comparison, not evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands four learned baselines to ten, adding Yue et al., ContrastPhys+, RhythmMamba, RhythmFormer, PhysFormer, and FactorizePhys. Supplementary Table 9 additionally compares proficiency estimation using HR predictions from PhysFormer and FactorizePhys. The eye/skin signal-processing baselines and main Table 5 comparator configurations already exist in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces bidirectional cross-dataset protocols, extracting eye regions with MediaPipe, resizing to 48 by 128, and converting to grayscale. Transfer experiments use the model without MITA because the conventional datasets lack head IMU recordings. The stated signal-processing baseline bandpass changes from 0.6-3.0 to 0.5-2.8 Hz. Existing participant splits and core training hyperparameters remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds explicit spatial-attention and MITA ablations, activity-specific MITA comparisons, cross-dataset generalization tests, HR-distribution analysis, and downstream HR-source comparisons. Conversely, v1 Supplementary Table 9 is removed, eliminating sensitivity results for preprocessing, image/window sizes, losses, target signals, and augmentation.

E5.justification: Supplementary Section 15 and Figure 6 newly report prediction-MAE distributions by cross-validation split and an overall interquartile range of 1.7-10.5 bpm. This adds descriptive variability reporting; neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The IMU-enabled model reports MAE 7.67 bpm and r=0.85, versus v1's video-only 8.82 and 0.81; the earlier aggregate scores remain as the no-MITA ablation. Activity and frame-rate results change, and substantial baseline, ablation, and transfer results are added. Table 5 changes overall Ego+Exo+HR accuracy from 42.37% to 43.94%, while Ego+HR remains 45.29%. These updates involve the revised model, rather than an unchanged-method performance comparison.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 adds a formal definition of IMU-image cross-attention, including its embedding dimensions and query/key/value assignments (Equation 3). The optical reflection model and spatial-attention mathematics remain equivalent; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace the central claim of HR estimation solely from eye-tracking video with a method that fuses video and built-in IMU motion cues. v2 also announces released code, data, and EgoExo4D HR augmentations. The egoPPG task, dataset contribution, and claimed 14.1% egocentric proficiency improvement remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets dancing improvements through MITA and explains residual static-task errors through HR variability, blinking, and eye motion. It adds hypotheses for soccer failures involving scarce examples and unseen stop-and-go activity, discusses transfer generalization, and introduces explicit consent requirements. These substantially expand the mechanisms and applicability boundaries discussed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project link and announces code, dataset, and HR-augmentation releases. It supplies MITA implementation details, cross-dataset preprocessing, peak-based HR extraction, feature normalization, and inference throughput. Reported model resources change from approximately 770k parameters, 164 GFLOPS per batch, and 15 training hours to 12M parameters, 399 GFLOPS, and 20 hours.

R1.justification: v2 refreshes the literature with additional rPPG competitors, prior spatiotemporal-attention methods, and OBF/SCAMPS, while removing several gaze and wearable-device citations. The introduction adds Project Aria 2's contact HR sensor as context. The fundamental positioning around recovering HR from headset cameras for egocentric tasks remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and substantial discussion passages are rewritten. Section 5 gains named component descriptions and reorganized experimental subsections; Section 8.3 becomes Broader impacts, with demographic and outdoor future work moved into the conclusion. The model is renamed throughout and the supplementary narrative is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn to depict IMU-image fusion. Table 2 expands substantially, and Table 3 replaces its RMSE/MAPE columns with a MITA comparison. The supplement adds three experimental tables and two boxplots while removing the hyperparameter table. Existing signal traces, photographs, and dataset/protocol tables are relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through stronger comparators, explicit component ablations, cross-dataset HR evaluation, and downstream HR-source comparisons (Tables 2-3 and 7-9). These address important gaps in v1's evidence for component benefits and generalization. Resource access information also improves reproducibility. Removing the hyperparameter study loses useful sensitivity evidence, and reporting inconsistencies remain, such as upsampled MAE 10.20 in the text versus 10.18 in Table 4. These drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger validation.
